body: Iran is drafting next year’s budget under the premise that oil revenue could fall to zero, with senior budget official Mohammad Ghasemi telling the government on Monday to prepare for that scenario, as the country appears to be weeks away from that eventuality. Iran has loaded no crude since August 25, according to the US Treasury, and the oil it held at sea outside the US blockade fell from 88.8 million barrels in mid-July to zero by mid-October. Chinese buyers pay one to two months after delivery, so Kpler expects that revenue could stop around mid-December. Oil accounts directly for roughly 30% of the government budget, according to Gregory Brew of Eurasia Group and Miad Maleki of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, and Maleki puts its share of total regime revenue at 50% to 60% once indirect income is counted. According to Chatham House’s Bilal Saab , “The Iranian leadership is betting that if it holds out long enough, those with the most to lose from this economic crisis – Saudi Arabia, the UAE, Qatar, and Kuwait – will press Washington harder to find an exit.” But Trump has settled, for now, on keeping the blockade in place without new strikes, and he says the Gulf states want the same. “Qatar, Saudi Arabia, UAE, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others, would prefer the status quo,” he said on Monday . Then, on Thursday, he said “we don’t need a deal with Iran” and removed Vice President JD Vance from the negotiations, closing the direct channel Vance had opened with a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council. Rezaei had welcomed the letter’s tone , then insisted that Washington accept Iran’s conditions first and said no enriched uranium would leave Iran. Mohammad Tabibian, who was deputy director of the Planning and Budget Organization under President Ali Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, told Shargh newspaper on Monday that endurance is the wrong measure of success. “Adapting to sanctions does not mean eliminating their harm,” he said. “A society can therefore gradually become poorer without experiencing a sudden halt to all economic activity.” So, an exit isn’t in sight, and Kpler puts Iranian oil production below 2 million bpd in the months before late October, down from 3.59 million in February, the month the war began. OPEC’s latest report puts Iranian output at almost half its pre-war level. The US naval blockade imposed on April 13 then emptied the oil Iran kept at sea. Crude and condensate held outside the blockade zone fell from 88.8 million barrels on July 14 to zero by mid-October, and another 43 million barrels remain stranded inside it. Maleki says Iran will run short of cash in December but will not collapse. “The December timeline is more of a cash flow kind of disruption, and not really a collapse state,” he told Fox News Digital in late October. He told Iran International that the serious trouble will start “when they can no longer pay the cost of buying and transporting the goods they are now importing over land.” Esfandyar Batmanghelidj, founder and CEO of the Bourse & Bazaar Foundation, calls it a recession. “Iran’s economy is not on the verge of collapse, it is simply experiencing a deep recession caused by an external shock,” he wrote on X on November 10, citing his foundation’s finding that the fall in non-oil output after six months of war was about one-seventh of Ukraine’s contraction after Russia’s invasion. Iran’s Statistical Centre put total GDP 10.1% lower year on year in the three months to June 20, with non-oil output down 4.6%, The National reported . Batmanghelidj also sees Tehran’s neighbours as a possible lifeline, writing a day later that regional countries “which can’t tolerate more instability” may “quietly support the Iranian economy, including by breaking the blockade.” Tehran’s plan for next year promises to keep paying salaries and pensions without printing money, but offers little to replace the oil income that paid for much of it. summary: President Donald Trump extended the Jones Act waiver for another 90 days on Friday, keeping foreign-flagged tankers eligible to move oil and other commodities between U.S. ports as the war with Iran continues to drive up fuel costs. body: Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… President Donald Trump extended the Jones Act waiver for another 90 days on Friday, keeping foreign-flagged tankers eligible to move oil and other commodities between U.S. ports as the war with Iran continues to drive up fuel costs. The extension, confirmed by a White House official who spoke to Reuters , continues what is already the longest waiver in the shipping law's history. Foreign vessels will still need approval for individual voyages due to a restriction introduced in August after earlier blanket exemptions drew opposition from the domestic maritime industry. The 1920 Jones Act requires cargo moving between American ports to travel on U.S.-built, U.S.-owned and U.S.-crewed vessels. Suspending that act allows for a much larger pool of ships. Phillips 66 was among the first to take advantage of the original waiver, shipping roughly 300,000 barrels of Bakken crude from Texas to Monroe Energy's Trainer refinery in Pennsylvania aboard the Malta-flagged HTM Warrior in April. The administration has since tightened the rules. Roughly 300 waivers were granted under the earlier blanket exemptions in March and May, compared with just 48 since the switch to individual approvals in August, according to government figures cited by Reuters . The White House hopes the additional shipping flexibility will help contain gasoline, diesel and fertilizer prices, although previous exemptions have delivered little relief at the pump. U.S. gasoline averaged $3.91 per gallon Thursday, compared with $2.98 before the Iran war began . Diesel stood at $6.10, up from $3.76, according to AAA. Shipping accounts for only a small portion of retail gasoline prices, and critics estimate that relaxing the Jones Act would save consumers mere pennies per gallon . More than 50 Republican lawmakers urged Trump in June to restore the restrictions, citing American maritime jobs and national security concerns. As it stands currently, shippers must prove that suitable American vessels are unavailable before getting approval for using foreign ships. The latest extension keeps that approval process intact. title: Freeport strikes $77M deal for BC copper stake
summary: Freeport has committed to spend $30 million of the $80 million exploration total within three years of closing.
body: Freeport-McMoRan (NYSE: FCX) has agreed to pay $77.2 million (C$110 million) for a controlling stake in TDG Gold’s (TSXV: TDG) Aurora West project in British Columbia, advancing consolidation around the neighbouring Aurora copper-gold discovery held by Freeport and Amarc Resources (TSXV: AHR). The initial purchase covers 51% of two companies that will hold the property, TDG said Thursday . Freeport can lift its stake by funding $80 million in exploration and paying TDG another $40 million. “Our retained interest in the Aurora West Property through the joint venture also gives our shareholders continued exposure to its upside potential,” TDG CEO Fletcher Morgan said. Proceeds from the deal will strengthen TDG’s cash holdings without issuing shares and help it advance its Shasta gold-silver project, Morgan said. The transaction could bring adjoining ground into the Freeport-Amarc partnership in the Toodoggone district. Amarc has rights to participate in acquisitions that fall wholly or partly within 2 km of the partnership’s property. TDG shares dropped 7% to 66¢ Friday morning in Toronto, valuing the company at about $186 million. They’ve traded between 39.5¢ and $1.11 over the past year. Freeport’s options would raise its stake to 75% in Aurora West JVCo and 100% in ClaimsCo, which holds two specified claims. TDG would retain 25% of the former and a 2% net smelter return royalty over the latter’s claims. Shasta and the Baker property are excluded from the sale. TDG won’t have to contribute to either company during the earn-in option period. If Freeport doesn’t exercize the option, it would retain 51%, with subsequent costs shared in proportion to ownership, subject to dilution. Freeport has committed to spend $30 million of the $80 million exploration total within three years of closing, including at least $15 million in the first two, TDG said. Completion requires TSX Venture Exchange approval. TDG expects the pre-closing reorganization in December, with closing five business days after conditions are satisfied or waived. Claims and other rights acquired wholly or partly within the area of common interest must be offered at cost to Aurora Minerals, the existing Freeport-Amarc joint venture, Amarc said in a separate announcement Thursday. TDG’s Aurora West drilling has focused on ground within that area, it said. Freeport owns 60% of Aurora Minerals and is earning another 10% by funding $75 million of staged spending. About $40 million to $45 million has already been spent. Amarc says Freeport must fund the first estimated $30 million to $35 million of applicable acquisition costs through the remaining earn-in expenditures. After Freeport reaches 70%, Amarc would fund its 30% share of applicable costs. Amarc awaits formal notice and would then have at least 45 days to elect to participate. It raised $20 million in September and has appointed Agentis Capital Mining Partners as financial adviser. Amarc separately announced completion of a $22-million exploration program at the 630-sq.-km Joy district. Freeport funded almost 14,000 metres of drilling in 16 holes, testing Aurora and other targets. Assays remain pending. The district is connected to Prince George by highways and resource roads serving the Kemess area. A 230-kilovolt transmission line runs alongside the resource road to the former Kemess South mine, according to Amarc’s project overview. Spare capacity may be available to other projects, the company says. Acquisition to expand the company's road construction capabilities to support future growth.

title: Mineros’ gold bet raises cash and collateral risks
summary: The strategy increases Mineros’ exposure to the metal beyond the gold it produces in Colombia and Nicaragua.
body: Mineros (TSX: MSA; US-OTC: MNSAF) bought $137.3 million of bullion in the third quarter and expanded its borrowing against physical gold, drawing an analyst warning that its treasury strategy is adding risk despite strong mining profits. The purchases pushed reported quarterly operating cash flow below zero, Mineros said Wednesday. Mineros ended September with $54 million in cash and $127.7 million in borrowings, then added gold-backed financing agreements that require additional cash collateral if prices fall, according to its quarterly filings. “We continue to view the treasury strategy negatively and now add margin call exposure to the risks,” Red Cloud mining analyst Alina Islam said Friday in a note. Mineros’ treasury strategy “is taking up a growing share of the balance sheet and adding leverage.” The strategy increases Mineros’ exposure to the metal beyond the gold it produces in Colombia and Nicaragua. Higher bullion prices could benefit its holdings, but a decline could create calls for cash at the same time weaker prices reduce mining revenue. The company’s explanation is that retaining exposure to gold aligns its treasury with investors who buy the shares for exposure to the sector. Management considers the holdings part of its capital-management policy, CEO Daniel Henao said. “This position reflects our view that gold remains an effective long-term store of value in the current macroeconomic environment,” Henao said in the results release. Mineros already had 15,601 oz. of gold tied to repurchase agreements at Sept. 30. Its Swiss subsidiary posted 20,000 oz. of gold on Oct. 16 for net proceeds of $73.2 million after an $8.7-million cash collateral deposit, followed by 8,981 oz. on Oct. 29 for $32 million. Repurchase obligations fall due in October 2027 and February 2027, respectively. Mineros guarantees the obligations and retains the exposure to changes in gold prices. Islam calculated that about 88% of the company’s physical gold was pledged under the agreements. That estimate combines September’s pledged gold with the October transactions and assumes no intervening changes in holdings or earlier agreements. Borrowings at the September quarter-end were more than eight times their level at the end of 2025, before the October transactions. The gold exposure also included a forward contract to buy 18,650 oz. at $4,740 per oz. As of Sept. 30, Mineros recorded a $10.5-million liability on that contract and had posted $12.5 million in cash margin. It also recognized an $11.9-million non-cash write-down on allocated bullion. The financing comes as shareholders prepare to vote on a special dividend of 20¢ a share, totalling about $58 million, at a Nov. 24 meeting. The proposal was announced Oct. 23, between the two gold-backed financing transactions. If approved, the payment would be made Dec. 4 to shareholders of record Dec. 1, in addition to the ordinary dividend. Mineros expects to fund it from cash on hand and operating cash flow. As of Sept. 30, the company also reported $145.4 million of unpledged precious metals in its net cash calculation, which put net cash at $71.7 million after borrowings. That company-defined measure treats available precious metals as cash equivalents for this calculation. The mining business delivered quarterly adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $140 million, 55% more than a year earlier, the company reported. Net income was $89.5 million, or 30¢ a share, compared with 18¢ a year earlier. The realized gold price averaged $4,301 per ounce. Reported operating cash flow was negative $21.6 million after bullion purchases. Before those purchases, the company’s operating cash flow before strategic gold purchases was positive $115.7 million. Quarterly gold production rose 13% to 62,253 ounces. Mineros’ full-year forecast stands at 235,000 to 245,000 oz., following an increase announced in October. Its Hemco plant expansion in Nicaragua is due for completion

body: Wall Street analysts downgraded Nvidia in a wave on Thursday, Nov. 12, as Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive and the company named CFO Colette Kress interim CEO ( our story ). Bernstein, Oppenheimer, Melius and William Blair all cut their ratings, and William Blair moved its preference to AMD [1] [2] [3] [4] . Nvidia shares were down 13% in early trading on Thursday after falling 16% from Nov. 3 through Wednesday, CNBC reported [4] ( our markets story ). Firm Old rating New rating Price target Bernstein Outperform Market perform Halved to $200 Oppenheimer Outperform Perform Removed Melius Buy Hold $315 to $185 William Blair Outperform Market perform None given Stifel Buy Buy $315 to $205 Citi Buy Buy $225 Bernstein downgraded the stock in a note late Wednesday. "We admit to struggling mightily with this call, and can sympathize with the case to buy the dip. But our gut tells us that we probably haven't yet fully probed the depths of what might be found here; we've had enough, and prefer to watch from the sidelines," the firm wrote [1] . Rasgon added that "the fundamentals of the business (if not the leadership) are clearly still intact" [2] . Oppenheimer said it was "downgrading shares of NVDA and removing our price target following reports (WSJ, NYT) of founding CEO Jensen Huang's imminent departure amidst allegations of a 2nd extramarital affair" [1] . Schafer called the departure "a material, potentially thesis-changing event" [2] . Melius said the stock trades at about 10 times next year's consensus earnings, which it called "extremely cheap", but that a strong pre-announced quarter or a bigger buyback "would not address long-term issues" [3] . Not everyone left. Stifel kept a buy rating while cutting its target to $205 from $315, Citi kept buy with a $225 target, and Mizuho, UBS and Raymond James held bullish ratings, according to Investing.com [2] . Baird downgraded Nvidia to neutral on Wednesday ( our coverage ). "Nvidia is facing increased scrutiny and a potential leadership vacuum, and while ASIC competition remains a risk to Instinct (particularly at Meta and OpenAI), we see an opportunity for AMD to benefit from custom programs as an opportunity for CPU attach," William Blair analyst Sebastien Naji wrote, in a note issued hours before Huang's resignation was announced [4] . Naji also pointed to delays in Intel 's Xeon roadmap and said AMD's lead is widening in a server CPU market he sizes at $220 billion by 2030 [4] . AMD shares have risen 37% over the past five days, and 48 of 56 analysts rate the stock a buy or strong buy, according to LSEG data cited by CNBC [4] . Nvidia reports fiscal third-quarter results on Nov. 17, its first under interim leadership; our pre-earnings look at the valuation is here .

AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
summary: The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers.
body: Threats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday. The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks. "Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated. The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling. Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election. Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed. Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion. The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.

title: Australia hikes rates to 18-year high to fight inflation
summary: The Reserve Bank of Australia's decision was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year.
body: Australia's central bank raised its benchmark cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.85% on Tuesday, the highest level since November 2008. The Reserve Bank of Australia's move was in line with expectations from economists polled by Reuters, and marked its fifth rate increase this year. In its statement, the RBA said that the move was a split decision, with six members voting for the increase and three opting for a hold. This also comes as the country continues to grapple with high inflation, with the consumer price index rising 4.3% in September, up from 4% in August and marking its highest level since March. The central bank also said inflation is now expected to "remain elevated through much of 2027," and not expected to fall back into its 2%-3% target range till late 2027, three quarters later than previously forecast. This was due to higher fuel and other commodity prices, in addition to factors including AI-related investment, which is driving rapid growth in prices for technology-related goods, the RBA said. In its September decision, RBA governor Michelle Bullock said that inflation is "too high," driven by higher oil prices from the Iran War and stronger domestic spending. "We're seeing signs that upside risks to inflation are materializing," she added, saying that additional hikes will come "if that's what's needed to get inflation down." Growth has slowed in the first two quarters of 2026. Australia's GDP rose 2.1% in the June quarter compared to a year earlier, down from 2.5% in the March quarter. The RBA is trying to bring inflation back under control while higher borrowing costs and cost-of-living pressures weigh on households and activity. When asked if she sees a recession for Australia, Bullock said that it is "not our base case at the moment."

body: The Federal Reserve is likely to accelerate the pace of interest rate hikes to rein in stubbornly high inflation , according to a growing number of Wall Street analysts. Aditya Bhave, a U.S. economist with BofA Global Research, expects monetary policymakers to raise the Fed's benchmark rate by 0.25 percentage points at each of the central bank's next three meetings in December, January and March. Analysts at TD Securities also predict three straight quarter-point hikes, up from their previous forecast of two, because hotter inflation signals that price pressures across the U.S. are broadening. The latest Consumer Price Index showed that inflation r ose more than expected in October, climbing 0.4%. "Inflation is not trending in the right direction," TD Securities said Friday in a note to investors. "The October report not only surprised our own forecast, it was also not driven by a particular factor or two as had been the case in recent reports. Price pressures appear to be broadening." Hotter inflation in October was the third straight month that prices have risen faster than expected amid supply constraints and ample economic demand, according to EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco, who is penciling in rate hikes for December and January. "For any borrower, this will mean a high cost of borrowing for any type of consumer loan people take out," Daco told CBS News. "A higher federal funds rate trajectory will generally mean higher long-term interest rates and increase the cost of borrowing for consumers across the country." Interest rate traders put the odds of a quarter-point hike at the Fed's next meeting on Dec. 8-9 at nearly 90%, and also see a better-than-even chance of another such hike at the Jan. 26-27 gathering, according to CME FedWatch . Some Fed officials themselves have said tightening may need to be more aggressive to bring inflation in line with their 2% annual target. At a conference in London on Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller said policymakers should consider a 0.50 percentage-point increase in December, adding that a smaller hike "would put our credibility at risk." High energy prices continue to drive inflation, along with robust corporate spending on data centers and other equipment for powering AI. "Together, these forces could keep inflation elevated into 2027 and weigh further on household purchasing power," Daco said in a report.

Producer prices rise, backing case for more Fed rate hikes - Finance & Commerce
body: U.S. producer prices increased 6.5% year over year in October, the fastest pace in four years, reinforcing expectations that the Federal Reserve may continue raising interest rates. Rising food, transportation and core goods costs signal persistent inflation pressures that could affect borrowing costs, business investment and consumer spending. WASHINGTON — U.S. producer prices rose moderately in October, but inflation at the factory gate posted its largest annual gain in four years, supporting the view that the Federal Reserve could continue raising interest rates after next month’s widely expected hike. Despite the better-than-expected monthly reading reported by the Labor Department on Friday, there were more signs of inflation broadening out beyond energy goods, with food prices increasing by the most in eight months as expensive diesel raised transportation costs. Prices of goods excluding food and energy logged their biggest gain since May. “There is no silver lining in the report,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “It looks like consumers will be on the hook for a fresh burst of consumer inflation. Everywhere you look, inflation is pushing forward and making the affordability crisis for Americans that much harder.” The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3% last month after an upwardly revised 1.4% surge in September, the Labor Department’s Bureau of Labor Statistics said. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the PPI climbing 0.4% after a previously reported 1.3% jump in September. The PPI shot up 6.5% year-over-year in October, the largest annual gain since November 2022, after advancing 6.3% in September. The report followed news this week of a stronger-than-expected increase in consumer prices in October. Producer prices over the month were lifted by a 0.5% rise in goods prices. Food prices vaulted 1.3%, the biggest increase since February, driven by fresh and dry vegetables, chickens, turkeys and beef as well as dairy products, confectionery goods and roasted coffee. Prices for basic organic chemicals increased 3.9%. Energy prices dipped 0.1%, amid a 7.9% decline in diesel fuel. Still, diesel fuel prices soared 115.2% on a year-over-year basis in October. “The diesel shock is still working its way through the economy even as those prices have eased into November,” said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. “Food prices are going to cause a further upset in consumer sentiment as they rise into the holidays and well into 2027.” The artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout is also exerting pressure on inflation. Prices for electronic components and accessories increased 4.2% over the month and accelerated 31.7% on a year-over-year basis. Though electronic computers and computer equipment prices were unchanged, they surged 21.4% in the 12 months through October. Excluding food and energy, producer goods prices increased 0.5% after gaining 0.3% in September. These so-called core goods prices accounted for more than 60% of the rise in overall producer goods prices last month. Goods prices advanced 10.2% in the 12 months through October, the biggest gain in four years. Transportation costs rise Services increased 0.2% after accelerating 1.0% in September. These prices have now risen for five straight months. A 2.0% increase in transportation and warehousing services costs, mostly freight transportation by road, accounted for three-quarters of the rise in services inflation. The cost of transporting freight by trucks accelerated 3.9%. Prices for fuels and lubricants retailing, health, beauty and optical goods retailing as well as food and alcohol wholesaling increased strongly last month. Hospital outpatient care prices rebounded 0.8%. Hotel and motel room prices increased 2.5%, while the cost of legal services fell 0.2%. Airfares dropped 1.2% even as jet fuel prices rose. title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns; Analyst Flags KYC Regulatory Risk, Cuts Price Target in Half - BigGo Finance
body: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as CEO and board member amid multiple extramarital affair scandals, and the company announced Thursday that 59-year-old Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take the helm on an interim basis. After the news broke, market doubts about the long-term prospects of the AI chip giant surged rapidly. Truist Securities fired the first shot on Friday, downgrading Nvidia from "Buy" to "Hold" and halving its price target to $174 from $346. Truist Managing Director William Stein noted in a report to clients that the damage from this episode goes beyond Huang's personal controversies or his departure itself — it lies in the possibility that Nvidia's corporate culture may already have been damaged, and in whether the company's graphics processors may have flowed to Chinese companies and government agencies, which will directly affect future revenue performance. He believes that Huang's association with a woman alleged to be a Chinese intelligence asset could highlight gaps across the industry in "know your customer" (KYC) compliance, and that the U.S. Department of Commerce may push related rules as a result. If that happens, it would compress Nvidia's future revenue scale and growth room. Stein further suggested that Nvidia's board should proactively establish mechanisms to ensure its AI products are only provided to entities whose identities the company has fully vetted. He acknowledged this is "a massive undertaking" requiring substantial new measures from both the company and its customers, but said that if Nvidia can take a leadership position in this area, it could be a remedial outcome from the storm. Succession Plan Unsettled; Market Names Multiple Possible Candidates Kress has served as Nvidia's CFO since 2013, having previously worked at tech giants including Microsoft, Cisco and Texas Instruments. People familiar with the matter said she has long been one of the few senior executives internally willing to check Huang's high-risk investment ambitions, and the two sides' teams clashed over massive financing deals involving OpenAI and AI infrastructure player Lambda. A plan originally intended to support OpenAI's construction of a data center in Ohio, sized at $250 billion, was ultimately scaled back to $120 billion. People who know Kress describe her as pragmatic and steady, in sharp contrast to the confrontational style Huang often displayed. As internal turmoil intensified, she has recently joined conference calls to reassure customers and suppliers. The market expects that under her leadership, Nvidia's handling of relations with Washington may turn more conciliatory, seeking to accumulate political capital rather than confronting the government head-on over chip export controls as it did during Huang's tenure. However, whether she, with her financial background, can carry on Nvidia's technological innovation and risk-taking spirit remains a major question mark. Moor Insights and Strategy chief analyst Anshel Sag said bluntly that having Kress serve as interim CEO to stabilize the market is "perfectly reasonable," but he does not think she is the long-term visionary leader Nvidia needs to maintain its current trajectory. The board is still searching for a formal successor, with Nvidia executive Ian Buck, AMD CEO Lisa Su and Arm CEO Rene Haas all named as potential candidates. Multiple Brokerages Cut Ratings; Near-Term Operations Still Supported Wall Street's reaction to the management earthquake has been polarized. KeyBanc Capital Markets analyst John Vinh believes Kress has deep internal knowledge of Nvidia's business and strategy, making her appointment as interim CEO a positive arrangement. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon also cut his price target to $200 from $400 and downgraded the stock from "Outperform" to "Market Perform," but stressed he is not worried about the past week's events hitting near-term operations and that Nvidia shares are indeed very cheap on a valuation bas
